mcqs.question: Why is finding a design flaw during threat modeling, before code is written, cheaper than finding the same flaw after launch?
options: Design-time findings require no engineering effort to fix at all
Threat modeling tools automatically generate the fix
Post-launch fixes only ever require a configuration change
The flawed assumption is still isolated to a whiteboard, rather than already baked into many call sites across the shipped code
mcqs.explanation: A flaw caught before implementation is one conversation; the same flaw caught after launch is usually replicated across every endpoint or call site that made the same bad assumption, on top of needing incident response and possibly disclosure. None of the fixes are free, but the cost multiplies with how deeply the assumption is embedded.

mcqs.question: A user can complete an action and later credibly claim they never did it, because there's no way to prove otherwise. Which STRIDE category does this describe?
options: Repudiation — the inability to prove who performed an action
Spoofing, since the user is pretending to be someone else
Tampering, since a record could theoretically be altered
Elevation of privilege, since the user gained an unintended capability
mcqs.explanation: STRIDE's R is specifically about the inability to attribute and prove an action after the fact — this maps directly to the non-repudiation gap covered in the CIA triad topic. Spoofing is about identity at the time of the action, not provability afterward, and the other two categories describe unrelated failure modes.

mcqs.question: When is an attack tree a better fit than a straight STRIDE pass over a data flow diagram?
options: When you want exhaustive coverage of every path to one specific, high-value goal, like full account takeover
When the system has no trust boundaries at all
When you only care about denial-of-service threats specifically
When the team wants to skip risk scoring entirely
mcqs.explanation: Attack trees start from a specific attacker goal and decompose every path to it, which is ideal when one asset matters enough to warrant exhaustive path coverage. STRIDE is the better fit for systematically sweeping threat categories across a whole diagram; the two techniques complement rather than replace each other.

mcqs.question: A team has already identified a shortlist of threats from a STRIDE pass and now needs to rank them by severity quickly. Which method is the most proportionate next step?
options: Running a full PASTA process from business objectives through simulated attacks
A lightweight DREAD-style or likelihood-times-impact scoring pass over the existing list
Re-running STRIDE a second time on the same diagram
Skipping scoring and fixing threats in the order they were discovered
mcqs.explanation: DREAD-style scoring exists specifically to take an already-identified threat list and rank it by severity with low additional effort — a good match for this situation. PASTA is a much heavier full methodology suited to business-critical systems, not a quick triage step, and fixing in discovery order ignores actual risk.

mcqs.question: In the worked login-flow example, why does the auth service enforce its own rate limiting even though the API gateway already rate-limits requests?
options: Rate limiting at the gateway is always disabled by default

Because complete mediation means every access should be checked at the point that matters, not assumed safe because an earlier layer claims to have checked it — an internal caller could bypass the gateway entirely
Because the auth service and gateway must always duplicate every control for compliance reasons
Because rate limiting is only effective when applied twice in sequence
mcqs.explanation: The auth service can't safely assume the gateway's rate limiting was actually applied to every request that reaches it, since an internal caller could reach the auth service directly. This is the same complete-mediation idea from Security Design Principles applied at the service level: don't trust a cached or upstream decision.

mcqs.question: A company threat-modeled its checkout flow at launch three years ago and hasn't revisited it since, despite adding two new third-party payment integrations. What's the risk?
options: The new integrations introduce trust boundaries the original model never considered, so their specific threats were never analyzed
There is no risk, since the original threat model covers all future changes automatically
The risk only applies if the original model contained errors
Threat models expire automatically after one year regardless of changes
mcqs.explanation: A threat model is a snapshot of the system as it existed when drawn; new integrations create new trust boundaries and data flows that were never walked through STRIDE. The fix is triggering a targeted re-review at specific events like new integrations, not treating the original document as permanently complete.
